sentences.text: Moabosaurus is a genus of turiasaurian sauropod dinosaur known for its thin, low neural spines and thick-walled vertebrae containing large pneumatic chambers. It possessed large, spatulate teeth similar to those of Camarasaurus and an ulna featuring well-developed ridges and a large olecranon process.
Although a 2017 description estimated the animal reached 10 meters long, this measurement was based on juvenile and sub-adult specimens, suggesting the adult may have been significantly larger.
Fossil evidence reveals that beetle larvae consumed portions of Moabosaurus bones before burial, leaving behind distinct mandible marks.

Named by Brooks B. Britt, Rodney D. Scheets, Michael F. Whiting, and D. Ray Wilhite, the species Moabosaurus utahensis was found at the Dalton Wells Quarry, located about 20 km northwest of Moab, Utah. Detrital zircon crystals date this site to 125 million years ago, indicating the dinosaur lived during the Aptian age.

Between 1975 and 2005, the quarry yielded parts of at least 18 individuals, totaling over 5,500 bones. Many of these remains are fragmentary due to intense trampling, evidenced by breakage and scratches.

The Dalton Wells quarry has yielded fossils of coexisting dinosaurs including the brachiosaurid Venenosaurus, theropods Utahraptor and Nedcolbertia, a tall-spined iguanodontian, and the ankylosaurian Gastonia.
Non-dinosaurian taxa at the site are rare and limited to fragments of a pterosaur, crocodilians, turtles, and a neochoristodere.
A 2017 analysis classified Moabosaurus as a basal titanosauriform macronarian neosauropod, while a second 2017 study placed it in the Turiasauria, outside of the Neosauropoda.
Moabosaurus shares derived features with Turiasaurus, including a specific braincase structure, bifurcated cervical ribs, low neural spines, and strongly procoelous proximal caudal vertebrae.

Moabosaurus utahensis is the only known species of extinct Moabosaurus, a titanosauriform sauropod that lived approximately 125 million years ago during the Barremian in what is now North America. The Paleobiology Database records the time range for the genus as the Valanginian, from 137.05 to 132.6 million years ago.
